b: ‘I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life’ (5:13). After a split in the church, John reassures the believers who stayed and warns them against those who left. He gives three tests that run through the whole letter, like a spiral: what you believe about Jesus, whether you obey God’s commands, and whether you love your fellow believers.

It is simple in language and deep in content: ‘God is light’, ‘God is love’, ‘We love because He first loved us’. It is unsettling for the complacent and unusually comforting for the anxious: ‘Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts’ (3:20).

The letter does not name its author, but its first readers clearly knew him, and he writes as an eyewitness: ‘which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands’ (1:1). Its language and themes are very close to John’s Gospel: light and darkness, truth, love, abiding, eternal life.

Early Christian writers consistently name the apostle John, author of the Gospel. Irenaeus (about AD 180), who as a young man heard Polycarp, a disciple of John, cites both the Gospel and 1 John as by ‘John, the disciple of the Lord’. Papias (early 2nd century) already used the letter. Eusebius (about AD 325) listed it among the books accepted by all, and said that ‘not only his gospel, but also the former of his epistles, has been accepted without dispute’.

Many scholars today accept John the apostle as author. Others think of a close disciple, John ‘the Elder’ (compare 2 John 1), or a circle of John’s followers. Most date the letters to the last decades of the 1st century, at Ephesus, where early tradition says John lived in old age; a few date them to the 60s.

hist.t: The people who ‘went out from us’
b: A group had left the church (2:19), and were trying to lead others astray (2:26). They denied ‘that Jesus is the Christ’ (2:22) and that ‘Jesus Christ has come in the flesh’ (4:2), and apparently claimed to know God and be without sin while not loving their fellow believers (1:6–10; 2:4, 9).

Their exact teaching is debated. Many scholars link them with early ‘Docetism’ (from a Greek word for ‘to seem’): the idea that the divine Christ only seemed to be human, which Ignatius of Antioch opposed in the same region a few years later (about AD 110). Irenaeus describes a teacher in Ephesus called Cerinthus, a rival of John, who taught that the divine ‘Christ’ came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross, so that only the human Jesus suffered. Irenaeus also records a story, from Polycarp, of John leaving a public bath-house when he learned Cerinthus was inside. Whether John’s opponents were Cerinthus’s followers or something similar, 1 John’s insistence that Jesus Christ ‘came by water and blood’ (5:6), that is, was the Christ at his baptism and at his death, fits such teaching well.

1.h: What we have heard and touched
1.t: John writes as a witness, against teaching that denied Christ came in a real body. The physicality is deliberate.

1.h: If we say we have no sin
1.t: Written to believers. Confession is presented as ongoing and normal, and the promise is that God is faithful and just — not merely merciful — to forgive.

2.t: Christ as defence counsel with the Father, and as the atoning sacrifice. John's aim in writing is that they would not sin, and his provision is for when they do.

John says Christ is the atoning sacrifice for our sins and also for the sins of the whole world. Reformed Christians have read that as the cross being sufficient for all and effective for those who believe; others read it as an atonement made equally for everyone and applied on condition of faith. The difference is real and it has never stopped either side preaching Christ freely to anyone who will listen. Note the pastoral setting: John raises it to comfort people who have sinned, not to settle a debate. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.
Not the created order or its people, but the system organised without God, defined by three desires that pass away.

3.t: See what kind of love — John's word carries astonishment. What we will be has not appeared yet, and the hope purifies now.
Defined by the cross and then measured by whether a man with means shuts his heart against a brother in need. John will not let love stay abstract.

4.t: Not every spiritual claim is from God, and the test given is doctrinal: what is confessed about Jesus come in the flesh.

The most quoted verse in the letter sits inside an argument, and the argument is that love is defined by the cross rather than by our intuitions about it. Verse 10 supplies the definition: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice.

5.t: Older English Bibles include a clause here about three heavenly witnesses. It appears in no Greek manuscript before the sixteenth century and modern translations rightly omit it. Nothing is lost: the Trinity is taught throughout Scripture without it.
The purpose of the whole letter. Assurance is presented as something believers may have, and the three tests running through the letter — belief, obedience, love — are how it is examined.

5.h: Can I know I am saved
5.t: John wrote this letter so that believers may know they have eternal life. Assurance does not rest on feelings, which come and go, but on three things John keeps returning to: believing that Jesus is the Son of God come in the flesh, a real if imperfect desire to obey him, and love for other Christians. The Reformed position is that those truly in Christ will persevere to the end because God keeps them. If you are anxious about whether you are really a Christian, that anxiety is itself worth bringing to someone who knows you. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

1.ctx: The opening echoes John’s Gospel (‘In the beginning was the Word’, John 1:1). Against people who denied that Christ truly came in the flesh, John stresses the physical reality of what the apostles experienced.
1.mean: ‘That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life.’ The eternal life ‘that was with the Father’ was revealed in a real human being. John proclaims it ‘so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ.’
1.big: The eternal Son of God became a real man whom the apostles saw and touched, so that we can share their fellowship with God.

1.ctx: The opponents seem to have claimed fellowship with God and freedom from sin while living carelessly. John answers each claim (‘If we say…’).
1.mean: ‘God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.’ Claiming fellowship with him while walking in darkness is a lie. ‘But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.’ ‘If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves’. ‘If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.’
1.big: Walking with God means honesty about sin, and confessed sin is forgiven and cleansed.
1.diff: ‘Faithful and just to forgive’. God is not merely kind to forgive, but ‘just’, because Christ’s blood has paid for sin (2:2). Confession. Protestants read verse 9 as confession directly to God, and often to one another (James 5:16). Catholic and Orthodox churches also practise confession to a priest in the sacrament of penance, and see this verse as including it.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 John (trans. Owen), CCEL

2.ctx: ‘Advocate’ (Greek paraklētos) is someone who stands beside you in court. In John’s Gospel the same word is used of the Holy Spirit.
2.mean: ‘I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.’ Real knowledge of God shows in obedience: ‘Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked.’
2.big: When believers sin, Jesus pleads for them as the sacrifice that turns away God’s anger, and true knowledge of him shows in obedience.
2.diff: ‘Atoning sacrifice’ translates hilasmos, traditionally ‘propitiation’ (BSB footnote): a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin. Some translations prefer ‘expiation’, a sacrifice that wipes away sin. See the glossary. ‘The whole world’. For whom did Christ die? Arminian (Wesleyan): for every person. Wesley: ‘Just as wide as sin extends, the propitiation extends also.’ Reformed: Christ’s death is sufficient for the whole world, but was intended to redeem effectually those the Father gave him (Canons of Dort, Second Head, arts. 3 and 8). Calvin knew the formula ‘Christ suffered sufficiently for the whole world, but efficiently only for the elect’, agreed with it, but said, ‘I deny that it is suitable to this passage’: John’s point, he thought, is that Christ is the Saviour of believers everywhere, not only of John’s first readers. Some Reformed theologians (sometimes called ‘four-point’ Calvinists or Amyraldians) hold that Christ died for all in one sense and for the elect in another. All agree on John’s purpose: no one who comes to Christ will find his sacrifice too small for them.

2.ctx: The command to love was ‘old’ (Leviticus 19:18; taught from the start of their Christian lives) and ‘new’ (Jesus gave it new depth, John 13:34).
2.mean: ‘If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is still in the darkness.’ ‘Whoever loves his brother remains in the light’. Then John reassures every age group: little children, ‘your sins have been forgiven through His name’; fathers, ‘you know Him who is from the beginning’; young men, ‘you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.’
2.big: Love for fellow believers is the sign of living in God’s light.

2.ctx: ‘The world’ here is not God’s creation, or the people he loves (John 3:16), but human life organised without God.
2.mean: ‘Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not from the Father but from the world. The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever.’
2.big: The world’s cravings and pride are passing away; doing God’s will lasts for ever.

2.ctx: ‘The last hour’ is the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings. See The people who ‘went out from us’ above.
2.mean: ‘Just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared.’ ‘They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us.’ The believers have ‘an anointing from the Holy One’ and know the truth. ‘Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son.’
2.big: Denying who Jesus is, is the mark of antichrist; and those who leave the truth show they never belonged.
2.diff: Antichrist. John is the only New Testament writer to use the word. He speaks both of a coming ‘antichrist’ and of ‘many antichrists’ already present: anyone who denies the Father and the Son. Christians differ on whether a single final figure is still to come (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). See the glossary. Verse 19 and perseverance. Reformed readers see here that those who finally leave the faith show they were never truly born again. Arminian readers note that John is describing these particular false teachers, and does not settle whether a true believer can fall away.

2.ctx: ‘Remain’ (or ‘abide’) is one of John’s key words (compare John 15).
2.mean: ‘Let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you. If it does, you will also remain in the Son and in the Father.’ ‘The anointing you received from Him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But just as His true and genuine anointing teaches you about all things, so remain in Him’. ‘Remain in Christ, so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming.’
2.big: Holding on to the original gospel, taught by the Spirit, is how believers remain in Christ.
2.diff: The ‘anointing’ is widely understood as the Holy Spirit. ‘You do not need anyone to teach you’ does not reject teachers (John is teaching them); it means they need no new teaching beyond the gospel they first received, which is what the false teachers were offering.

3.ctx: This passage contains some of the hardest verses in the letter, on whether believers sin.
3.mean: ‘Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are!’ ‘When Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is. And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself’. ‘No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning.’ ‘This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil. Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God.’
3.big: God’s children share his nature, and so cannot settle into a life of sin.
3.diff: Does a Christian sin? In 1:8 John says, ‘If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves’; here he says a child of God ‘cannot go on sinning’. Most interpreters, helped by the present tense (which the BSB brings out: ‘keeps on sinning’, ‘practice sin’), take this to mean a settled pattern of life, not every single sin. Calvin: John ‘does not make the children of God wholly free from all sin’, but ‘the design of regeneration is to destroy sin’. Wesleyan theology reads it more strongly: a believer, while faith remains, need not commit wilful sin; Wesley wrote that ‘the divine seed of loving faith abideth in him; and, so long as it doth, he cannot sin, because he is born of God.’ This is part of Wesley’s teaching on Christian perfection. Both agree that new birth makes a real change, and that John wants believers neither complacent about sin nor despairing over it.

3.ctx: Cain (Genesis 4) is the first murderer and the opposite of love.
3.mean: ‘We should love one another. Do not be like Cain’. ‘We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers.’ ‘By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers. If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?’ ‘Let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.’ When our consciences accuse us: ‘Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things.’
3.big: Love is shown in practical self-giving, and God is greater than our accusing hearts.
3.diff: Verse 20 is a deep comfort for the over-sensitive conscience. John does not say ‘your heart is wrong to accuse you’; he says God knows everything, including our faith and love, and his verdict is greater than our feelings.

4.ctx: ‘Spirits’ here means people who claim to speak by the Spirit: prophets and teachers.
4.mean: ‘Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world.’ The test: ‘Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God.’ ‘Greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.’
4.big: Spiritual claims must be tested by what they say about Jesus.
4.diff: The test was aimed at teachers who denied Christ’s real humanity. Christians have applied it more widely: any teaching must be judged by whether it is faithful to the Jesus of the apostles, truly God and truly man. That includes teachers who are impressive, popular or claim special revelation.

4.ctx: The high point of the letter.
4.mean: ‘Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God.’ ‘Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.’ ‘This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.’ ‘There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear’. ‘We love because He first loved us.’ ‘For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen.’
4.big: God is love, shown supremely in sending his Son as a sacrifice for us; our love is the response.
4.diff: ‘God is love’ does not mean ‘love is God’, or that God is only love. John also says ‘God is light’ (1:5). And John defines love by the cross: not our feelings, but God giving his Son ‘as the atoning sacrifice for our sins’. Many theologians have also seen here a hint of the Trinity: love needs someone to love, and the Father has loved the Son from eternity (John 17:24).

5.ctx: ‘Water and blood’ probably answers teachers who said the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism (water) but left before his death (blood). See The people who ‘went out from us’ above, and The ‘Johannine Comma’ below.
5.mean: ‘Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God’. Loving God means keeping his commandments, ‘And His commandments are not burdensome’. ‘This is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith.’ Jesus Christ is ‘the One who came by water and blood… not by water alone, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies to this’. ‘For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood—and these three are in agreement.’
5.big: Faith in Jesus as the Son of God, truly baptised and truly crucified, is what overcomes the world.
5.diff: ‘Water and blood’ has been read as (1) Jesus’ baptism and his death, which fits the opponents’ teaching best; (2) the water and blood from his side at the cross (John 19:34); or (3) baptism and the Lord’s Supper. These are not exclusive, and many see more than one meaning.

b: The King James Version reads at 5:7–8: ‘For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth’. These words (called the ‘Johannine Comma’, from a word for a short clause) are not in modern translations; the BSB gives them in a footnote.

The evidence is clear. The words are missing from nearly all manuscripts. They first appear in Latin manuscripts, probably as a marginal comment that a later copyist took into the text. No Greek manuscript of any kind has them before about AD 1215, and the earliest Greek manuscript to include them in the text itself is from the 14th century; only eight late Greek manuscripts out of about 5,800 have them at all, four of those only in the margin. None of the early church fathers who defended the Trinity in the great 4th-century debates quotes them, which they surely would have if they had known them. Erasmus left them out of his first two printed Greek New Testaments; after he was shown one Greek manuscript containing them (probably made to order), he added them in his third edition of 1522, and from there they entered the King James Version. Calvin, working from the printed editions of his day, was unsure but inclined to accept them; his 19th-century editor noted that they are not found in any Greek manuscript before the 16th century.

Nothing is lost. The doctrine of the Trinity was confessed by the church for over a thousand years before these words appeared in a Greek Bible, and rests on many other passages (for example Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14; John 1:1; 1 Corinthians 12:4–6).

5.ctx: In a court, evidence was established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).
5.mean: ‘Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater.’ ‘And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.’
5.big: Eternal life is found in God’s Son, and nowhere else.

5.ctx: John states his purpose for the whole letter (compare the purpose of the Gospel, John 20:31).
5.mean: ‘I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life.’ We can pray with confidence: ‘If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us.’ If someone sees a fellow believer committing a sin ‘not leading to death, he should ask God, who will give life’. ‘There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin.’
5.big: Believers can know they have eternal life, and can pray confidently for one another.
5.diff: Assurance. John wants believers to ‘know’ they have eternal life. Reformed (Westminster Confession 18) and Wesleyan traditions both teach that believers can have real assurance, though they explain its basis differently (the Reformed stress God’s promises and keeping; Wesley stressed the inner witness of the Spirit, Romans 8:16). ‘A sin that leads to death’ is not explained. Calvin took it to be ‘apostasy, by which men wholly alienate themselves from God’, like the teachers who had left; he rejected using this verse for a distinction between ‘venial and mortal sin’, and warned against rashly judging anyone beyond hope. Catholic teaching does use this passage in distinguishing mortal and venial sin: ‘Sins are rightly evaluated according to their gravity’ (Catechism 1854). Others suggest it is a sin bringing physical death as discipline (compare 1 Corinthians 11:30). All agree that John is not telling believers to stop praying for one another.

5.ctx: Three closing statements of what ‘we know’, and a final warning.
5.mean: ‘We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning; the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him. We know that we are of God, and that the whole world is under the power of the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true; and we are in Him who is true—in His Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols.’
5.big: Believers know the true God through his Son, are kept by him, and must keep away from every substitute.
5.diff: ‘He is the true God’. Grammatically ‘He’ could refer to the Father or to Jesus Christ, the nearest name. Calvin applied it to Christ: ‘It applies, indeed, most suitably to Christ’. Many interpreters agree, which makes this one of the New Testament’s plain statements that Jesus is God (compare John 1:1; 20:28). ‘Keep yourselves from idols’ is an abrupt ending: anything put in place of the true God, including a false Christ, is an idol.
